region: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea — slow streams, ponds and ditches
description: The wild form of the cherry shrimp: mottled, see-through olive to brown, often with a pale stripe down the back, camouflaged on plants and leaf litter. Females carry 20–30 eggs under the abdomen for 3–4 weeks, and the young hatch as miniature shrimp with no larval stage.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A line-bred Neocaridina selected for a deep, even cobalt blue from rostrum to tail fan, with the best animals blue on the legs as well. Crossed with other color lines, its offspring soon revert toward brownish wild-type colors.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A blue Neocaridina line with a lighter, more matte cobalt color than Blue Dream. Color intensity varies with grade, and like all Neocaridina colors it looks deeper on a dark substrate.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A Neocaridina line whose sky-to-deep-blue color sits over a glassy, semi-translucent body, giving the "jelly" look rather than a solid opaque blue. Females color up far more strongly than males.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A Rili-pattern Neocaridina: blue on the head and tail with a clear, colorless band across the middle of the abdomen. Grading rewards a cleanly defined clear section, and each brood includes young with more or less blue.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A Rili-pattern form of the cherry shrimp with a red head and tail and a clear, colorless band across the middle of the abdomen. It is as hardy as other Neocaridina colors and breeds freely in a planted tank.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A yellow Neocaridina with an opaque, metallic golden-yellow stripe running the length of its back. As in other yellow lines, females are much more intensely colored than the paler males.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A solid, bright orange color line of Neocaridina davidi. Like other color lines, it is most intense in mature females and fades when the shrimp is stressed or kept over pale sand.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A green Neocaridina line ranging from olive to bright jade, one of the newer and less stable colors. Good lines are evenly green over the body and legs.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A solid black Neocaridina with a glossy, near-opaque shell. Juveniles hatch lighter and darken as they grow, and males stay a little duller than females.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A solid chocolate-brown color line of Neocaridina davidi, opaque from rostrum to tail fan. Males and juveniles are a lighter brown.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A deep, glossy crimson Neocaridina developed in Taiwan. Its red is carried in the body tissue rather than in shell chromatophores, so the shrimp looks lacquered and slightly see-through rather than chalky.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A high grade of red Neocaridina, above Cherry and Sakura, in which body and legs are a solid, opaque red with no clear patches. The very best are sold as Painted Fire Red.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Taiwan, eastern China & Korea)
description: A pale, whitish-translucent Neocaridina named for its round white egg clutches, which look like tiny snowballs under the female’s tail. It is among the hardiest color forms but shows little color.

region: Southern China — cool hill streams in Guangdong & around Hong Kong
description: The wild ancestor of the crystal shrimps, banded black and white like a bee and living among leaf litter in cool, soft hill streams. Long traded as Caridina cantonensis, it was described as a separate species in 2014; its eggs hatch directly into tiny shrimp.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: southern China — Guangdong & Hong Kong)
description: A red-and-white form of the bee shrimp, bred in Japan by Hisayasu Suzuki from a red mutant he found in the early 1990s. Grading rewards dense, opaque white and sharply defined red bands; it needs the same cool, soft, acidic water as its wild ancestor.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: southern China — Guangdong & Hong Kong)
description: The black-and-white counterpart of the Crystal Red: a selectively bred bee shrimp with bright, opaque white and jet-black bands. Black is dominant over red, so crossing the two gives black young that carry the red gene.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: southern China — Guangdong & Hong Kong)
description: A solid, opaque white form of the bee shrimp in which the white pigment covers the whole body and hides the bands; the purest grades are sold as Snow White. Breeders have used it to strengthen the white in crystal red lines.

region: Captive-bred, Taiwan (wild form: southern China — Guangdong & Hong Kong)
description: A Taiwan Bee variety: a solid, glossy blue-black bee shrimp without the white bands of its crystal ancestors. Taiwan Bees arose from crystal-shrimp breeding in Taiwan and need the same cool, very soft water.

region: Captive-bred, Taiwan (wild form: southern China — Guangdong & Hong Kong)
description: A Taiwan Bee variety with broad, solid black bands on a bright white body, bolder and more opaque than a Crystal Black. It is bred and graded alongside King Kong and Blue Bolt in very soft, acidic water.

region: Captive-bred, Taiwan (wild form: southern China — Guangdong & Hong Kong)
description: A Taiwan Bee variety colored an opaque sky blue to icy blue-white. High grades carry the blue evenly from rostrum to tail fan, including the legs.

region: Captive-bred, Taiwan (wild form: southern China — Guangdong & Hong Kong)
description: A Taiwan Bee variety colored a solid, deep wine red without white bands, the red counterpart of the Black King Kong. Like other Taiwan Bees it is kept in soft, acidic water over an active soil.

region: Southern China — hill streams in Guangdong
description: A stream shrimp with a clear to amber body crossed by thin black "tiger" stripes along the abdomen. Long traded as a form of Caridina cantonensis, it was described as a separate species in 2014; the young hatch as miniature shrimp.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: southern China — Guangdong)
description: A captive-bred tiger shrimp line with a deep blue body, fine black tiger stripes and bright orange eyes. Only part of each brood colors up fully blue; the rest are paler or wild-colored.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: southern China — Guangdong)
description: A captive-bred tiger shrimp line whose body darkens to near-solid black, so the stripes show only faintly. It is sold with either black or orange eyes; orange-eyed animals are the more sought after.

region: Southern China — Hong Kong & Guangdong hill streams
description: An orange stream shrimp with fine dark tiger stripes along the abdomen, sold under the name Caridina serrata. Trade stock is now mostly captive-bred, ranges from yellow-orange to deep tangerine, and breeds readily in soft to moderately hard water.

region: India — streams and ponds
description: A small Indian stream shrimp found in green, brown and striped forms, able to lighten or darken with its surroundings and diet. It breeds in fresh water, and the eggs hatch directly into miniature shrimp.

region: Indo-West Pacific — lower courses of coastal rivers, India & Sri Lanka to Indonesia & the Philippines
description: A slender, glassy shrimp with a long, upturned red rostrum, also called the Pinocchio shrimp. It lives in the lower reaches of coastal rivers and its larvae need brackish water, so it does not breed in a freshwater aquarium.

region: Indo-West Pacific — coastal island streams from the Ryukyus & Taiwan to Indonesia & the Pacific islands
description: A stocky shrimp with a finely toothed rostrum that can change color within minutes, from red to brown, green or near-black, often with a pale stripe down the back. It is amphidromous: the larvae drift out to sea, so it does not breed in fresh water.

region: Sulawesi, Indonesia — Lake Matano (endemic)
description: Endemic to ancient Lake Matano, where it grazes biofilm on rocks and stones. Its cardinal-red body is dotted with white and its legs are tipped white; it needs warm, alkaline water and produces only small broods.

region: Sulawesi, Indonesia — Lake Towuti (endemic)
description: Endemic to Lake Towuti, where it lives on rocky bottoms. Its dark, partly translucent red-brown body carries bright yellow patches on the rostrum and cheeks, hence the trade names Yellow Nose and Yellow Cheek.

region: Sulawesi, Indonesia — Lake Towuti (endemic)
description: An endemic of Lake Towuti that lives on rocks in shallow water. It is brown to red with white patches and a conspicuous white band across the abdomen, and was sold as Caridina sp. "Red Orchid" before its description in 2009.

region: Sulawesi, Indonesia — Lake Towuti (endemic)
description: A tiny shrimp that lives only on freshwater sponges in Lake Towuti, one of very few freshwater shrimps known to live as a commensal. Its whitish, partly clear body is patterned with red-brown bands and spots that blend with the sponge.

region: Southeast Asia — rivers and streams from Thailand & Malaysia to Indonesia & the Philippines
description: A filter-feeding shrimp that perches in strong current and opens four fan-like brushes on its front legs to catch drifting particles, sweeping them to its mouth. It is amphidromous, with larvae that need brackish water, so it is not bred in home aquaria.

region: West & Central Africa and northeastern South America — rivers
description: Despite its name a harmless filter feeder, it stands in the current with its fan-tipped front legs spread to strain food from the water, and picks over the bottom when the flow is weak. Its color can shift between molts from cream or pinkish brown to blue-grey; it does not breed in fresh water.

region: South & Southeast Asia to northern Australia — rivers, lakes & estuaries
description: One of the largest freshwater prawns and farmed across the tropics; dominant males grow enormous blue claws longer than their body. It is a nocturnal predator that will catch sleeping fish, and its larvae need brackish water.

region: Thailand, Malay Peninsula & Myanmar — ponds, ditches and rice fields
description: An almost completely transparent prawn with a few dark lines on the head, common in still and slow waters of mainland Southeast Asia. Unlike many prawns it breeds in fresh water, and adults will catch small shrimp and fish fry.

region: Eastern USA — coastal-plain lakes, swamps and slow streams, New Jersey to Texas
description: A nearly transparent grass shrimp of fresh coastal-plain waters, sold in vast numbers as feeder and clean-up shrimp (now often placed in the genus Palaemon). Females carry greenish eggs that hatch into tiny free-swimming larvae, which can be raised in fresh water.

region: Mexico — Lake Pátzcuaro, Michoacán (endemic)
description: A dwarf crayfish known only from the highland Lake Pátzcuaro basin in Michoacán, where wild animals are mottled grey-brown. Females carry a few dozen eggs under the tail for three to four weeks, and the young hatch as miniature crayfish.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Lake Pátzcuaro, Mexico)
description: A captive-selected orange form of the Pátzcuaro dwarf crayfish and the most popular nano crayfish. It largely ignores healthy plants and adult fish, but will catch shrimplets and sleeping small fish.

region: USA — lower Mississippi Valley & Gulf coastal plain swamps and ditches
description: A small swamp crayfish of the lower Mississippi and Gulf coast, grey to rust-brown with a dark wavy band along each side of the abdomen. It is short-lived but breeds readily, females carrying a few dozen eggs.

region: Central Mexico — highland lakes, canals and ditches
description: A robust dwarf crayfish of central Mexico’s highland lakes and canals, mottled grey-brown to olive with dark speckling. Females grow a little larger than males and carry their eggs under the tail until they hatch as miniature crayfish.

region: USA — southern Alabama & Mississippi, vegetated streams and swamps
description: The smallest crayfish in the hobby, barely 2.5 cm long and marbled in brown, tan and bluish tones. It is the most peaceful of the dwarf crayfish and generally leaves fish and adult shrimp alone.

region: South-central USA & northeastern Mexico — swamps, ditches and rivers (invasive worldwide)
description: The crayfish of Louisiana crawfish boils, now invasive across Europe, Asia, Africa and South America. In aquaria it uproots and eats plants, burrows, and catches fish, so it is best kept alone.

region: USA — peninsular Florida wetlands, including the Everglades
description: A crayfish of Florida’s seasonally flooded marshes that survives the dry season in burrows. Wild animals are usually brown with dark spots; the vivid blue aquarium form was bred from rare naturally blue individuals.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: southern Florida)
description: A captive-selected, intensely blue line of the Everglades crayfish and one of the most popular aquarium crayfish. Like the wild form it is territorial, uproots plants and will catch fish.

region: Captive origin — German aquarium trade, 1990s (invasive in Europe & Madagascar)
description: An all-female crayfish that reproduces by parthenogenesis, every animal a genetic clone of its mother; it arose from the slough crayfish Procambarus fallax and was first noticed in the German aquarium trade in the 1990s. Released animals have formed invasive populations in Europe and Madagascar.

region: Northern Australia & southern New Guinea — rivers and billabongs
description: A large, comparatively placid tropical crayfish farmed for food; mature males carry a bright red patch on the outer edge of each claw. It feeds mostly on detritus and plants but will catch slow fish at night.

region: Southeastern Australia — Murray–Darling basin rivers, farm dams and swamps
description: A hardy burrowing crayfish that survives drought by digging deep into drying farm dams and creek beds. Its color varies widely, from olive-brown to black or blue, and it tolerates cooler water than tropical Cherax.

region: Western New Guinea (West Papua), Indonesia — streams
description: A mid-sized Cherax from western New Guinea, described in 2006, whose whole body is an even apricot to salmon orange. As in other Cherax, females carry the hatched young under the tail until they are ready to forage alone.

region: Papua New Guinea — Fly River drainage
description: A New Guinea crayfish with dark and pale bands across the head-shield and tail, which gives it the trade name Zebra. It hides for much of the day and feeds largely on dead leaves and detritus.

region: West Papua, Indonesia — streams
description: One of the most colorful crayfish, with a pink head-shield shading to greenish grey, a dark blue-black tail edged in cream, and blue claws with pale margins. It was described in 2015 from animals already exported for years as Cherax sp. "Hoa Creek".

region: Central Java, Indonesia — forest streams
description: A small semi-terrestrial crab from central Java with a purple body and legs, pale claws and glowing yellow eyes, sold for years before it was described in 2015. Females carry their eggs until they hatch directly as tiny crabs, so there is no sea-going larval stage; it needs a paludarium with land.

region: Central Java, Indonesia — forest streams
description: A Javan vampire crab with a dark, almost black carapace, red-orange legs and claws and yellow eyes, described in 2015 together with G. dennerle. It spends most of its time on land near water, and the young hatch as miniature crabs.

region: Thailand — slow rivers, among the roots of floating plants
description: One of the smallest freshwater crabs, with a carapace under 1 cm, living among the dangling roots of floating water hyacinth. Fully aquatic and shy, it filters and picks fine particles with its hairy legs and rarely breeds in aquaria.

region: Sulawesi, Indonesia — Malili lakes (Matano & Towuti)
description: A fully aquatic crab from the ancient Malili lakes of Sulawesi, cream to orange-tan with bold black leopard spots. It is territorial and will catch fish and shrimp, so it is best kept singly or in a large species tank.

region: Sulawesi, Indonesia — Lake Matano (endemic)
description: Endemic to Lake Matano, this deep purple crab specializes in crushing the lake’s endemic snails but also scavenges carrion and plant debris. It is very territorial, and a single pair needs a tank at least a meter long.

region: Lake Tanganyika (endemic) — rocky shores
description: The largest of the crabs endemic to Lake Tanganyika, living among rocks; its heavy claws crush the lake’s thick-shelled snails, which have evolved armored shells in response. It is kept singly, often alongside Tanganyikan cichlids in hard, alkaline water.

region: Indo-West Pacific — mangroves and estuaries, India to Japan & Indonesia
description: A semi-terrestrial mangrove crab (now often placed in Parasesarma), olive to purplish brown with bright red claws, often sold as a freshwater crab although it does best in slightly brackish water with a land area. Its larvae develop in the sea, so it is not bred in aquaria.

region: Indo-West Pacific — fast coastal streams, Philippines & Indonesia to the western Pacific islands
description: A large nerite with a smooth, glossy, helmet-like shell in black to dark olive, often worn pale at the apex. It grazes biofilm in fast coastal streams; the larvae drift to the sea, so its egg capsules never hatch in fresh water.

region: Florida, the Gulf coast & Caribbean — coastal springs, rivers and estuaries
description: A small nerite of Florida and Caribbean coastal springs and estuaries, olive green with fine dark lines and flecks. Like most nerites it lays hard white egg capsules on rocks and glass that do not hatch in fresh water.

region: Philippines & Indonesia (Sulawesi & Maluku) — coastal streams and estuaries
description: A nerite whose shell is marked with bold black zigzag stripes, like tire tracks, over a red, orange or golden ground, the pattern differing from snail to snail. It lives in coastal streams and estuaries and does not breed in fresh water.

region: Indo-West Pacific — coastal streams and estuaries, Indonesia & the Philippines to the western Pacific
description: A small, round nerite banded in yellow and black, with a crown of spines around the top of the shell that can wear down or break with age. Like other nerites it lays white egg capsules that need brackish water to develop.

region: Indo-West Pacific — fast coastal streams, southern Japan & the Philippines to Indonesia
description: A flat, limpet-shaped nerite whose shell has almost lost its coil, an adaptation for clinging to rocks in strong current; the trade name comes from the dark bat-like marking on many shells. The olive to yellow-brown shell is netted with dark purple-black markings; it grazes biofilm and does not breed in fresh water.

region: Indo-West Pacific — lower courses of rivers and estuaries, India to the Philippines & New Guinea
description: A large snail with a glossy, jet-black, long-spired shell, living where coastal rivers meet the sea. It grazes biofilm and detritus and often burrows partly into soft sand; it does not breed in a freshwater aquarium.

region: Thailand & Myanmar — clear, fast streams over limestone
description: A dark brown snail whose tall shell is ringed with rows of spines, like the tiers of a pagoda. It needs clear, well-oxygenated, flowing water, and females brood their young and release them as tiny crawling snails.

region: Sulawesi, Indonesia — ancient lakes
description: A large Sulawesi lake snail with a dark, tall, ridged shell and a bright orange body; the long snout and drooping tentacles give rabbit snails their name. Females give birth to a single large, fully formed young at a time, released in a white capsule at long intervals.

region: Africa, the Middle East & southern Asia to northern Australia (introduced worldwide)
description: A tall, cone-shelled snail that spends the day burrowed in the substrate, turning it over and eating detritus, and comes out at night to graze. Most populations are all-female and parthenogenetic, brooding live young, so a few snails soon become hundreds.

region: South & Southeast Asia (introduced in the Americas, Africa & elsewhere)
description: A trumpet-like snail with a shorter, broader shell covered in rows of small granules, which give it a quilted look. Like Melanoides it is parthenogenetic and broods live young, and it has become invasive in many warm regions.

region: Southeast Asia — rivers and lakes of Thailand, Malaysia & Indonesia
description: A predatory snail that hunts other snails, pushing a long proboscis into the prey’s shell, and also scavenges carrion; it spends much of the day buried with only its siphon showing. Females lay single eggs in small capsules on hard surfaces, and the young burrow for months after hatching.

region: Amazon basin — Bolivia, Brazil & Peru
description: The wild form of the aquarium "mystery snail", long sold as Pomacea bridgesii: a tan to olive-brown shell with dark spiral bands. It breathes air through a long siphon raised to the surface and lays clutches of pale pink eggs just above the waterline; unlike some apple snails it rarely damages healthy plants.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Amazon basin — Bolivia, Brazil & Peru)
description: A captive color form with a bright yellow, unbanded shell over a pale, gold-flecked body. It is the mystery snail most often seen in pet shops.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Amazon basin — Bolivia, Brazil & Peru)
description: A captive color form with a creamy white, unbanded shell and a pale, gold-flecked body. Its shell shows algae and mineral deposits more than darker colors.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Amazon basin — Bolivia, Brazil & Peru)
description: A captive color form in which a dark body shows through a translucent blue-grey shell; faint darker banding is often still visible.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Amazon basin — Bolivia, Brazil & Peru)
description: A captive color form with a very dark brown to black shell over a dark body; in strong light the shell often shows deep brown banding.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Amazon basin — Bolivia, Brazil & Peru)
description: A captive color form with a thin shell tinted purple to plum over a dark body; it can look nearly black until light catches the shell from the side.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Amazon basin — Bolivia, Brazil & Peru)
description: A captive color form with a pinkish red to magenta shell over a pale body; the depth of color varies from snail to snail.

region: Northern South America (introduced in Florida, the Caribbean & elsewhere)
description: A large apple snail with a flat, ram’s-horn coiled shell banded dark brown on gold. A voracious plant-eater, it has been released to control water weeds and the snail hosts of schistosomiasis, and it lays clear jelly egg masses under water.

region: South America — southern Brazil to Uruguay & northeastern Argentina
description: A small apple snail, only about 3 cm across, whose golden-brown shell is striped with dark zigzag bands. Besides algae and detritus it eats the eggs of other snails, and it often digs itself into the substrate.

region: Florida, USA — springs, lakes and canals
description: A small, flat-coiled pulmonate snail from Florida that grazes algae and detritus and lays small jelly egg clutches on plants and glass. Its blood carries hemoglobin, which shows as a red body in the pale aquarium color forms.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Florida)
description: A color form of the Seminole ramshorn that lacks dark body pigment, so its hemoglobin-rich blood shows bright red through a translucent brownish-red shell. It is the red ramshorn usually sold in North America.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Florida)
description: A pale-shelled color form of the Seminole ramshorn in which the red, unpigmented body glows through a translucent pink shell.

region: Europe & western Asia — weedy ponds, ditches and slow rivers
description: Europe’s largest ramshorn snail, with a thick, dark olive-brown shell up to about 3.5 cm across. It thrives in cool, hard water and lays flat jelly egg clutches on plants and stones.

region: Captive-bred (wild form: Europe & western Asia)
description: A red color form of the great ramshorn that lacks dark pigment, so its hemoglobin-rich blood colors the body bright red under a translucent reddish-brown shell. It is the red ramshorn usually sold in Europe.

region: North America (now cosmopolitan)
description: A small, thin-shelled, left-coiling snail that hitchhikes into aquaria on plants and multiplies quickly wherever food is plentiful. It often glides upside down beneath the water surface and can lower itself on a thread of mucus.

region: Holarctic — ponds, lakes and slow rivers of Europe, northern Asia & North America
description: A large air-breathing pond snail with a tall, sharply pointed spire, a staple of school biology and a model animal in neuroscience. It eats plants as well as algae and carrion, and lays sausage-shaped jelly egg masses on leaves.

region: East Asia — China, Korea & Japan (invasive in North America)
description: A large, olive-green pond snail that can seal its shell with a horny lid, kept in garden ponds and coldwater tanks. Females give birth to live, fully formed young, and introduced populations have spread through North American lakes.
